I have been farming this land in Quzhou for forty years, ever since I was a young bride brought to this village. At sixty-seven, my back is not what it used to be, but my hands and eyes still know the soil here better than any book. We are eight mouths in my household, so I cannot afford to gamble everything on one crop, but the prompt says my cropping system is stevia, and that is the truth—stevia is the crop that pays the school fees and the medicine bills. Still, I keep wheat and maize because a farmer who does not grow her own grain is a farmer who sleeps hungry when prices fall. I have a well, which means I can irrigate, but electricity for the pump costs money, so I count every drop.

This year I will divide my 10.9 mu the same way I have for the last several seasons: 3 mu for the wheat-maize rotation, 3.5 mu for stevia, 2.4 mu for cotton, and 2 mu for millet. The wheat goes in after the National Day holiday, and come early June, as soon as the wheat comes off, I plant maize without turning the soil—no-tillage saves time and keeps moisture in the ground during the hot summer. The stevia I transplant in mid-April; it is my main cash crop and I give it the most water, five irrigations through the season, and plenty of compound fertilizer because it is a heavy feeder. Cotton I plant in spring as well; it needs fifteen sprays for bollworms and aphids, which is a lot of work with the backpack sprayer, but the price at the gin is steady. I put millet on the drier corner of the field—it only needs one irrigation and little pesticide, and the grain is good for porridge and the stalks for the chickens.

I use improved wheat seed (Luyuan 502) and hybrid maize (Denghai 605) because after all these years I know they do not fail me in our North China Plain weather. For cotton I use Guoxinmian, an improved variety, and for stevia I use Chengguang, which the buyer prefers. Millet I sow from my own traditional seed saved from last year. I till the wheat, cotton, stevia, and millet plots with the rotary tiller, but the maize gets no tillage after wheat. On fertilizer, I follow what the township ag-tech station taught me twenty years ago and what my own eyes confirm: wheat needs the most nitrogen, maize needs a top-dressing after the jointing stage, and stevia needs balanced N-P-K to make the leaves sweet.
